explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus says, "You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces." They don't walk in themselves, and they don't let in those who wish to enter. Picture someone standing in a doorway, not going through and not stepping aside either. That's a line nobody wants to be stuck behind.

explanations.answer: Open it only to their friends
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, but the text never mentions a favored few getting in. Jesus says they "shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces." He also says they won't let in those who wish to enter. So the door is closed, with no special list in sight.

explanations.answer: Sell a place in it to the rich
explanations.explanation: Money never comes up in these verses. Nobody is selling anything and nobody is holding a price tag. Jesus says they "shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces." The picture is a closed door, plain and simple.
It's actually the other way around, friend. Jesus says, "You yourselves do not enter." So they're standing outside the door too. And on top of that, He says they won't let in those who wish to enter.

Right. Jesus says, "You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter." So they stay outside, and they block the way for others. That's a double lockout. It's like me standing at my oven refusing to bake, and shooing everybody else away from the dough.

explanations.answer: Twice as much a son of hell as they are
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are." That's a heavy line, so I'll let it stand just as He said it. They travel land and sea for one convert, and this is what Jesus says that effort produces.

explanations.answer: A teacher twice as wise as they are
explanations.explanation: Wise would be nice, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says they make the convert "twice as much a son of hell as you are." So the convert doesn't come out wiser at all. It's a heavy woe, and the text says it plainly.

explanations.answer: A servant who carries all their loads
explanations.explanation: No servants or loads show up here. Jesus only says they make the convert "twice as much a son of hell as you are." The long trip by land and sea is in the verse, but what it produces is the part Jesus points at. That's the part to remember.

Gold it is. Jesus quotes their rule: "if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath." So in their rule the temple itself means nothing, but the gold on it binds you. Jesus calls them "blind guides" for it. Then He asks which is greater.

Doors sound like a reasonable pick for a temple, but they're not in this verse. The rule Jesus quotes is about "the gold of the temple." Swear by that, and you're bound by your oath. Doors don't come up at all.

A lampstand sounds fancy enough to fit, but it isn't what Jesus quotes. The rule is about "the gold of the temple." That's the thing that binds you to your oath. The lampstand never makes an appearance in this passage.

explanations.answer: The temple makes the gold sacred
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus asks, "Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred?" The gold only counts as sacred because of the temple. So treating the gold as the bigger deal gets it backwards. That's like valuing the sprinkles over the cookie, which I'll admit I've done on a hungry day.

explanations.answer: The temple cost more than the gold
explanations.explanation: Cost never comes up. Jesus says the temple is the one "that makes it sacred," and that's about the gold. So the question is about what makes something sacred, not what it cost. The answer is sitting right inside His question.

explanations.answer: The temple is older than the gold
explanations.explanation: Age isn't mentioned here at all. Jesus gives a different reason. He calls the temple the one "that makes it sacred," meaning the gold. That's why the temple is greater.

True. Jesus says, "he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it." So the gift on the altar isn't some separate thing the oath skips over. It all gets folded into one oath. That's Jesus answering their rule in one sentence.

Jesus actually says the opposite. He says, "he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it." So the gift on the altar is included, not left out. The oath covers the altar and all that sits on it.

Throne. Jesus says, "he who swears by heaven swears by God’s throne and by the One who sits on it." So even swearing by heaven points straight to God. There's no word in that oath that stands apart from Him.

Footstool is a real Bible word, friend. Isaiah, the prophet, calls the earth God's footstool in Isaiah 66:1. But in this verse Jesus says heaven means "God’s throne and the One who sits on it." So the word here is throne.

Name sounds holy enough to fit, but Jesus doesn't use it in this verse. He says swearing by heaven means swearing by "God’s throne and by the One who sits on it." The word that finishes the sentence is throne.

Yes. Jesus names them: "justice, mercy, and faithfulness." He calls these the weightier matters of the law. Then He says they should have practiced these, "…without neglecting the former." So He's lifting up the heavy things and not tossing out the small ones.

Those are all familiar words, but Jesus doesn't list them here. The weightier matters He names are "justice, mercy, and faithfulness." That's what He says they have disregarded while they tithe their herbs.

None of those are on Jesus' list in this verse. He says the weightier matters of the law are "justice, mercy, and faithfulness." Those are the ones He says they've disregarded. The herbs are the lighter side of the scale.

Not quite. Jesus says they should have practiced justice, mercy and faithfulness, "…without neglecting the former." The former is the tithing of mint, dill and cumin. So He isn't telling them to stop. He wants the weightier things added.

Right. Jesus says they should practice justice, mercy and faithfulness, "…without neglecting the former." So the tithing of mint, dill and cumin stays, and the weightier things join it. It's an and, not an or. In my bakery I need the timer AND the dough.

explanations.answer: They fuss over tiny things and miss huge ones
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel." A gnat is tiny and a camel is enormous. They're careful about the small thing and miss the giant one. Jesus has just named what they've disregarded, justice, mercy and faithfulness, so I think that's the camel.

explanations.answer: They keep every rule both big and small
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite. Jesus says they "swallow a camel," so they aren't keeping every big one. A couple of verses back, He said they have disregarded the weightier matters of the law. They're careful with the gnat and careless with the camel.

explanations.answer: They care more about animals than people
explanations.explanation: Animals are in the picture, but they're not the point. The gnat and the camel stand for tiny and huge. Jesus calls them "blind guides" because they strain at the small thing and swallow the big one.

Yes. Jesus says they clean the outside of the cup and dish, "but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence." The outside looks good and the inside tells a different story. Think of a mug that looks spotless until somebody checks the bottom.
Fear and laziness aren't on Jesus' list. He says the cup and dish are "full of greed and self-indulgence." The cleaning on the outside is real, and the trouble is hidden inside.
Those could sound like they'd fit, but they aren't the words Jesus uses. He says inside they are "full of greed and self-indulgence." That's what's inside the cup and dish.

True. Jesus says, "Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well." Inside first, and then the outside follows. He's speaking to one Pharisee in that verse. The order is the whole point.

It's true, actually. Jesus says, "First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well." So the inside comes first, and the outside follows. That's the card's claim, word for word.

Yes. The tombs look beautiful on the outside, but inside they're full of "dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity." It's a heavy picture, so I'll leave it plain. Looking nice outside and being something else inside is exactly what Jesus is pointing at.

Grain and oil would be a welcome thing to find stored somewhere, but Jesus is talking about tombs. He says they're full of "dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity." That's the inside of the picture.

Gold and jewels would be quite a surprise inside a tomb, but that isn't what Jesus says. He says the tombs are full of "dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity." They look beautiful outside, and that's where the beauty stops.

True. Jesus says, "on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness." So looking righteous and being righteous are two different things. He says it in plain words right after the tomb picture.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, "on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness." The card says the same thing in nearly the same words. He's spelling out what the whitewashed tombs meant.

explanations.answer: They're sons of those who murdered the prophets
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets." They had said they wouldn't have joined in. Jesus says their own words testify the other way. The murder of prophets is heavy, so I'll say it straight.

explanations.answer: They've never read what the prophets wrote
explanations.explanation: Reading isn't what Jesus is talking about. They say they wouldn't have been partners in shedding the prophets' blood. Jesus answers that they testify against themselves that they are "the sons of those who murdered the prophets."

explanations.answer: They want the prophets' places of honor
explanations.explanation: Jesus does talk about places of honor earlier in this chapter (Matthew 23:6), but that's not this verse. Here He says they testify against themselves that they are "the sons of those who murdered the prophets." That's what their own words say.
Hell. Jesus asks, "How will you escape the sentence of hell?" That's a heavy question, so I'll leave it just as He said it. Right before it, He calls them "snakes" and a "brood of vipers."
A council is an earthly court, and that's a natural guess. But Jesus doesn't name one here. He asks, "How will you escape the sentence of hell?" That's the sentence He means.
A governor would be an earthly authority, and Jesus doesn't mention one in these verses. He asks how they will escape "the sentence of hell." That's the word that finishes His question.

Abel. Jesus says, "from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah." Abel's story is in Genesis 4:8, where his brother Cain killed him. So Jesus reaches from the very first killing in the Bible to Zechariah, who was murdered between the temple and the altar.
Seth was born to Adam and Eve after Abel died (Genesis 4:25). But Seth isn't the name Jesus gives. He says, "from the blood of righteous Abel." Abel is where the list begins.

Noah, the man who built the ark, is called righteous in Genesis 6:9. But that isn't who Jesus names here. He says the blood runs "from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah." So Abel is the one at the start.

explanations.answer: A hen gathering her chicks under her wings
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, "how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings." It's a close, gentle picture. I think it's one of the tenderest lines in the whole chapter.

explanations.answer: A shepherd carrying lambs in his arms
explanations.explanation: A shepherd with lambs is a lovely picture, and Isaiah, the prophet, uses it for the LORD in Isaiah 40:11. But here Jesus chooses a different one. He says He longed to gather them "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings."

explanations.answer: An eagle carrying its young on its wings
explanations.explanation: Eagles' wings do show up in Scripture. In Exodus 19:4, God says He carried Israel on eagles' wings. But in this verse Jesus uses a different bird. He says, "as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings."
Jesus actually says the opposite. He says how often He has longed to gather them, "but you were unwilling!" So the longing was there, and the willingness wasn't. That's what the text says.
Right. After saying how often He longed to gather them, Jesus says, "but you were unwilling!" So the longing is there and the willingness isn't. I think that's the tender, sad part of this verse.
Yes. Jesus says, "you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’" The words begin with "Blessed." So the words Jesus names are words of blessing.
Sorrow is an easy guess after such a heavy chapter. But the words Jesus names are different. He says, "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord." That's a blessing.

Apology is a reasonable thing to expect, but it isn't what Jesus says. He names these words: "Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord." They begin with "Blessed," so they're words of blessing.
